rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers answer for faithfully delivering revelation and their people's response; nations answer for their conduct despite receiving a warner, as 7:6-7 describes.
rows.anchor: The accountability of the nation will be about what they have done in spite of the coming of a warner to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final accounting rewards messengers and their companions and punishes rejecters; this assures Muhammad and his companions and threatens his opponents with God's final judgment.
rows.anchor: one day, the whole case will be presented in the court of God and there one will come to know who won and who lost.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refutes idolaters' claim that God directed them to worship other deities: God's messengers are the source for knowing His directives, and earlier messengers can be consulted.
rows.anchor: This verse refutes the claim of the Idolaters that those whom they worship because God has directed them to do so.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to ask those sent before means consulting their teachings and Books; this is a subtle style found in earlier scriptures and eloquent orations.
rows.anchor: This style is often employed in earlier scriptures, and its examples can also be found in the orations of eloquent orators.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses and Pharaoh account supplies historical evidence for the divine retribution announced in 43:41-42: a rejecting nation's fate is decided, and Pharaoh and his army drowned despite their power.
rows.anchor: after a nation denies its messenger, its fate is necessarily decided whether in this own lifetime or after his migration or death.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account exemplifies 43:40: those who ruin their intellect and choose error remain blind to even great miracles until God's punishment opens their eyes.
rows.anchor: people who ruin their faculties of intellect and deliberately adopt the path of error are not guided by any sign.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account confirms 43:45: every messenger called people to monotheism, never to worship another deity, as the Qur'an does.
rows.anchor: all messengers of God called people to the very monotheism the Qur’ ān is calling them to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs given to Moses included the staff and the white hand; the Pharaoh's ملأ were his nobles and chiefs who attended his court.
rows.anchor: These included the staff and the white hand among others.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse summarizes Moses' address; elsewhere it is detailed as a warning that he was God's messenger, with signs, seeking permission to take the Israelites to a desert three days away for worship.
rows.anchor: at other instances, it is stated in detail that he informed the Pharaoh and his courtiers that he has been sent by God to them to warn them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A contextual clause is omitted: after hearing Moses claim prophethood and cite proofs, the Pharaoh's court demanded signs; Moses showed them, but they mocked them as tricks and boasted of superior magicians.
rows.anchor: Thus Moses (sws) showed them these signs; however, instead of acknowledging these signs, they made fun of him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With an omitted incomplete verb supplied, the verse means God kept sending increasingly exemplary warning signs after the initial signs were rejected, hoping Pharaoh's people would turn and repent.
rows.anchor: We kept on showing them one sign greater than the other so that they can turn to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people were so hard-hearted that no sign affected them until decisive punishment overtook them.
rows.anchor: no sign could influence them until they became the targets of the decisive punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When punishment struck, they pleaded with Moses to pray for its removal and promised to accept his message; once it was lifted, they broke their promise and returned to their old ways.
rows.anchor: However, when the Almighty would take away the punishment from them, they would break their promise and become adamant on their old ways.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning plagues included floods, locusts, lice, frogs, and blood; 7:133-135 recounts their arrogance, plea for relief, and broken promise to accept the message and free Israel.
rows.anchor: So, We sent on them the floods and locusts and lice and frogs, and blood as elucidated signs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Moses “Sorcerer” was respectful in that Egyptian society, where magicians and sorcerers held the standing that scholars and Sufis have in a society.
rows.anchor: This address, thus is an address of respect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about God's prior promise means that He promised to grant Moses' prayer, so Moses could invoke that promise when asking God.
rows.anchor: The implication is that since the Almighty has promised that He will grant the prayer of Moses (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reads لَمَّا as ف and says the following ذ, which signals suddenness, is apt in this construction.
rows.anchor: For this reason, the mention of ذ which connotes suddenness ( mufājāh) is very appropriate here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh proclaimed his possession of Egypt and its canals as Moses' miracles and arguments shook his people's devotion; the author compares this to Quraysh leaders' objection about the Qur'an's recipient.
rows.anchor: he made an announcement among his people that the kingdom of Egypt and its running canals are in his possession

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted argument contrasts Pharaoh's wealth and power with Moses, whom he disparages as a poor-speaking member of an enslaved nation, and asks what qualified him for prophethood.
rows.anchor: then what is in this person that God made him a messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the common understanding of 20:27, Moses did not stammer; he was simply not a forceful orator, a weakness Pharaoh used to challenge his leadership.
rows.anchor: however, he was not a forceful orator

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh argues that a genuine envoy should have gold bracelets and angelic escorts; Moses' apparent poverty was presented as evidence against his claim.
rows.anchor: why should God’s messenger come in such a state of indigence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gold bracelets and accompanying bands signified royal grandeur in the courts of Egypt and Persia, much as royal displays do today.
rows.anchor: in those times kings, particularly of Egypt and Persia would wear gold bracelets to display their grandeur and majesty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb istakhafa is opposite to istathqala: Pharaoh treated his people as simpletons, lured them, and they followed foolishly.
rows.anchor: like fools it was entrapped by him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their disobedience and lack of faith left them spiritually insignificant and easy for Satan to lead; a person gains weight through relationship with God.
rows.anchor: A person becomes weighty by his relationship with God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word أَسَفَ means to anger someone; the verse says the people angered God, so He took revenge on them.
rows.anchor: ie he angered him. The verse says that when they
